title: Part 1, Chapter 40
paragraphs: In which the captive's story continues
SONNET

"Blessed souls, set free from this mortal husk, rewarded for brave deeds and exalted, you now dwell above this lowly globe of ours, made heirs of heaven and immortality. With noble rage and burning ardour, while your strength was yours, you plied it in battle, and with your own blood and the enemy's stained the sandy soil and the encircling sea. It was the ebbing life-blood that failed your weary arms first; the stout hearts never quailed. Though defeated, you still earned the victor's crown: though mourned, your fall was still a triumph, for there, between sword and wall, you won glory in heaven and renown on earth."
"That is exactly it, as I recall," said the captive.
"Well then, the one about the fort," said the gentleman, "if my memory serves me, goes like this:"
SONNET

"Up from this wasted soil, this shattered shell, whose walls and towers lie here in ruin, three thousand soldier souls took wing on high to dwell in the bright mansions of the blessed. They tried in vain, with all the strength of their arms, to repel the enemy's onslaught, and when at last nothing remained but to die, the last defenders fell, wearied and few. And this same arid soil has always been the haunt of countless mournful memories, as much in our day as in days of old. But never yet, I think, has it sent to heaven from its hard bosom purer souls than these, or borne braver bodies on its surface."
The sonnets were not disliked, and the captive was glad of the news they gave him of his comrade. Continuing his tale, he went on:

With La Goletta and the fort now in their hands, the Turks gave orders to dismantle La Goletta — the fort was reduced to such a state that there was nothing left to level — and to do the work faster they mined it in three places. But nowhere were they able to blow up what seemed the weakest part, that is, the old walls, while everything left standing of the new fortifications the Fratin had built came down with the greatest ease. Eventually the fleet returned victorious and triumphant to Constantinople, and a few months later my master, El Uchali — otherwise Uchali Fartax, which in Turkish means "the scabby renegade" — died. He certainly was scabby; it is the Turks' custom to name people from some defect or virtue they possess, the reason being that among them there are only four surnames belonging to families tracing descent from the Ottoman house, and the rest, as I said, take their names and surnames from either bodily blemishes or moral qualities. This "scabby one" rowed at the oar as a slave of the Grand Signor's for fourteen years, and when he was past thirty-four, in resentment at having been struck by a Turk at the oar, he turned renegade and renounced his faith in order to take his revenge. And such was his valour that, without rising by the base methods most of the Grand Signor's favourites use, he came to be king of Algiers and afterwards general at sea, which is the third position of trust in the realm. He was a Calabrian by birth and a worthy man morally, and he treated his slaves with great humanity. He had three thousand of them, and after his death they were divided, as he directed in his will, between the Grand Signor (who is heir of all who die, sharing with the dead man's children) and his renegades. I fell to the lot of a Venetian renegade who, as a cabin boy on a ship, had been captured by Uchali and was so loved by him that he became one of his most favoured boys. He turned into the cruellest renegade I ever saw: his name was Hassan Aga, and he grew very rich and became king of Algiers. With him I went there from Constantinople, rather glad to be so much nearer Spain — not that I planned to write to anyone about my unhappy lot, but to try whether fortune would be kinder to me in Algiers than in Constantinople, where I had tried in a thousand ways to escape without ever finding the right moment or chance. In Algiers I resolved to look for other means of carrying out the purpose I cherished so dearly, for the hope of regaining my liberty never deserted me. When my plots and schemes and attempts did not turn out as I expected, instead of giving way to despair I would immediately look for or invent some new hope to keep me going, however faint or feeble it might be.

In this way I went on living, shut up in a building or prison the Turks call a baño, where they confine their Christian captives — those of the king's, those of private owners, and those they call "of the Almacen," meaning slaves of the municipality, who work on the city's public works and other jobs. Captives of this last kind recover their liberty only with great difficulty, because, being public property and having no particular master, there is no one to negotiate ransom with even if they have the means. To these baños, as I said, certain private individuals of the town are in the habit of bringing their captives, especially when they are being held for ransom, because there they can keep them safely and comfortably until the ransom arrives. The king's captives held for ransom likewise do not go out to work with the rest of the crew, unless their ransom is delayed; then, to make them write more urgently, they are forced to work and gather wood, which is no light labour.

I, however, was one of those held for ransom, because when it was discovered that I was a captain, although I declared my meagre means and lack of fortune, nothing would persuade them not to count me among the gentlemen and those awaiting ransom. They put a chain on me, more as a mark of this than for safekeeping, and so I passed my life in that baño with several other gentlemen and persons of quality singled out as held for ransom. Although at times — or rather almost always — we suffered from hunger and inadequate clothing, nothing distressed us so much as seeing and hearing at every turn the unparalleled and unheard-of cruelties my master inflicted on the Christians. Every day he hanged a man, impaled another, cut off someone's ears — all with so little provocation, or with none at all, that even the Turks acknowledged he did it just for the sake of doing it, since he was by nature murderously disposed towards the entire human race. The only one who fared at all well with him was a Spanish soldier, someone de Saavedra by name, to whom he never gave a blow himself or ordered one given, or addressed a harsh word, although he had done things that will dwell in the memory of the people there for many a year — all to recover his liberty. For the least of the many things he did, we all dreaded he would be impaled, and he himself feared it more than once; and only because time does not allow, I could tell you now things that soldier did which would interest and astonish you far more than the narration of my own tale.

To go on with my story: the courtyard of our prison was overlooked by the windows of the house of a wealthy Moor of high position. As is usual in Moorish houses, these were loopholes rather than windows, and besides were covered with thick, close lattice-work. It happened, then, that one day I was on the terrace of our prison with three other comrades, passing the time by seeing how far we could leap with our chains. We were alone, all the other Christians having gone out to work. I happened to raise my eyes, and from one of those little closed windows I saw a reed appear with a cloth attached to the end of it, and it kept waving and moving as if making signs to us to come and take it. We watched it, and one of those with me went and stood under the reed to see whether they would drop it or what they would do, but as he did so the reed was raised and moved from side to side, as if saying "no" by a shake of the head. The Christian came back, and the reed was lowered again, making the same movements as before. Another of my comrades went, and the same thing happened to him as to the first, and then the third went forward, with the same result. Seeing this I did not want to miss my own chance, and as soon as I came under the reed it was dropped and fell inside the baño at my feet. I hurried to untie the cloth, in which I noticed a knot, and inside it were ten cianis, which are coins of base gold current among the Moors, each worth ten reals of our money.

Needless to say I rejoiced over this windfall, and my joy was matched by my wonder as I tried to imagine how this good fortune could have come to us, and especially to me — for the evident unwillingness to drop the reed for anyone but me showed that the favour was intended for me. I took my welcome money, broke the reed, and returned to the terrace. Looking up at the window, I saw a very white hand put out, which opened and shut very quickly. From this we gathered, or imagined, that it must be some woman living in that house who had done us this kindness, and to show that we were grateful we made salaams in the Moorish fashion, bowing the head, bending the body, and crossing our arms on our chest. Shortly afterwards, at the same window, a small cross made of reeds was put out and immediately withdrawn. This sign led us to believe that some Christian woman was a captive in the house, and that it was she who had been so kind to us; but the whiteness of the hand and the bracelets we had glimpsed made us dismiss that idea. We thought instead that it might be one of those Christian renegades whom their masters often take as lawful wives, and gladly, since they prefer them to the women of their own nation. In all our guesses we were wide of the truth. From then on our sole occupation was watching and gazing at the window where the cross had appeared, as if it were our pole-star. But at least fifteen days passed without our seeing either it, or the hand, or any other sign. Meanwhile, though we tried with all our might to find out who lived in the house, and whether there was any Christian renegade in it, no one could tell us anything more than that the man living there was a rich Moor of high position called Hadji Morato, formerly alcaide of La Pata, an office of high dignity among them. But when we least expected any more cianis to rain from that quarter, we suddenly saw the reed appear again, this time with another cloth tied in a larger knot, and this at a moment when, as before, the baño was deserted and empty.

We tried as before, the same three going forward before me; but the reed was delivered to no one but me, and on my approach it was let drop. I untied the knot and found forty Spanish gold crowns and a paper written in Arabic, with a large cross drawn at the end. I kissed the cross, took the crowns, and returned to the terrace, and we all made our salaams. The hand appeared again, I signed that I would read the paper, and then the window was closed. We were all puzzled but filled with joy at what had taken place; and since none of us understood Arabic, our curiosity to know what the paper contained was great, and the difficulty of finding someone to read it even greater. At last I decided to confide in a renegade, a native of Murcia, who professed great friendship for me and had given pledges binding him to keep any secret I might entrust to him. It is the practice with some renegades, when they intend to return to Christian territory, to carry around certificates from notable captives stating, in whatever form they can, that such-and-such a renegade is a worthy man who has always shown kindness to Christians and is eager to escape on the first opportunity. Some obtain these testimonials with good intentions, others put them to cunning use: when they go raiding on Christian territory, if they are wrecked or captured they produce their certificates and say that these papers show why they came — to remain on Christian ground — and that this is why they had joined the Turks in their raid. By this means they escape the consequences of the first outburst and make peace with the Church before it does them any harm, and then, when they have the chance, they return to Barbary to become what they were before. Others, however, do procure these papers and use them honestly, and remain on Christian soil. This friend of mine was one of those renegades I have described: he had certificates from all our comrades, in which we testified for him as strongly as we could; and if the Moors had found the papers they would have burned him alive.

I knew he understood Arabic very well, and could not only speak but also write it; but before I disclosed the whole matter to him, I asked him to read for me this paper which I had, I said, found by accident in a hole in my cell. He opened it and spent some time examining it and muttering to himself as he translated. I asked him whether he understood it, and he said he did perfectly, and that if I wanted him to tell me its meaning word for word, I must give him pen and ink so that he could do it properly. We at once gave him what he asked for, and he set about translating it bit by bit. When he had finished he said:
"All that is here in Spanish is what the Moorish paper contains, and you must remember that when it says 'Lela Marien' it means 'Our Lady the Virgin Mary.'"
We read the paper, and it ran like this:

"When I was a child my father had a slave who taught me to say the Christian prayer in my own language, and told me many things about Lela Marien. The Christian woman died, and I know she did not go to the fire but to Allah, because since then I have seen her twice, and she told me to go to the land of the Christians to see Lela Marien, who has great love for me. I do not know how to go. I have seen many Christians, but except for you none has seemed to me a gentleman. I am young and beautiful, and have plenty of money to bring with me. See if you can contrive how we may go, and if you wish you shall be my husband there, and if not it will not distress me, because Lela Marien will find me someone to marry me. I myself have written this: take care to whom you give it to read; trust no Moor, for they are all treacherous. I am greatly troubled about this, because I would not have you confide in anyone — if my father knew of it he would at once throw me down a well and cover me with stones. I will tie a thread to the reed; fasten the answer to it, and if you have no one to write for you in Arabic, tell it to me by signs, for Lela Marien will make me understand you. May she and Allah and this cross, which I often kiss as the captive woman told me to, protect you."

Judge, sirs, whether we had reason to feel surprise and joy at the words of this paper. Both were so great that the renegade realised the paper had not been found by chance but had really been addressed to one of us; and he begged us, if his suspicion was correct, to trust him and tell him everything, because he would risk his life for our freedom. So saying, he took from his breast a metal crucifix and, with many tears, swore by the God it represented — in whom, sinful and wicked as he was, he truly and faithfully believed — to be loyal to us and to keep secret whatever we chose to reveal to him; for he thought, and almost foresaw, that through the woman who had written that paper he and all of us would obtain our liberty, and he himself would obtain what he so much desired, his restoration to the bosom of Holy Mother Church, from which by his own sin and ignorance he was now severed like a corrupt limb. The renegade said this with so many tears and such signs of repentance that we all agreed unanimously to tell him the whole truth, and so we gave him a full account, hiding nothing. We pointed out the window at which the reed had appeared, and by this means he took note of the house and resolved to find out with particular care who lived in it. We also agreed it would be wise to answer the Moorish lady's letter, and the renegade, without a moment's delay, took down the words I dictated, which were exactly what I shall tell you — for nothing of importance in this affair has escaped my memory, or ever will while life lasts. This, then, was the answer sent back to the Moorish lady:

"May the true Allah protect you, Lady, and that blessed Marien who is the true mother of God, and who has put it in your heart to go to the land of the Christians, because she loves you. Beg her to be pleased to show you how you can carry out what she commands, for she will, such is her goodness. On my part, and on the part of all these Christians with me, I promise to do all we can for you, even to death. Do not fail to write to me and tell me what you mean to do, and I will always answer; for the great Allah has given us a Christian captive who can speak and write your language well, as you can see from this paper. So without fear you can tell us anything you wish. As to your saying that if you reach the land of the Christians you will be my wife, I give you my promise on it as a good Christian; and know that Christians keep their promises better than the Moors do. May Allah and Marien his mother watch over you, my Lady."

With the paper written and folded, I waited two days until the baño was empty as before, and immediately took my usual walk on the terrace to see if there was any sign of the reed, which was not long in appearing. As soon as I saw it, although I could not make out who was holding it, I showed the paper as a sign to attach the thread; but the thread was already fixed to the reed, and to it I tied the paper. Shortly afterwards our star once more appeared with the white flag of peace — the little bundle. It was dropped, I picked it up, and found in the cloth, in gold and silver coins of all sorts, more than fifty crowns, which fifty times over strengthened our joy and doubled our hope of gaining our liberty. That very night our renegade returned and said he had learned that the Moor we had been told of did live in that house, that his name was Hadji Morato, that he was enormously rich, that he had one only daughter who was heiress to all his wealth, and that it was the general opinion throughout the city that she was the most beautiful woman in Barbary. Several of the viceroys who came there had sought her in marriage, but she had always been unwilling to marry. He had also learned that she had had a Christian slave woman who was now dead — all of which agreed with the contents of the paper. We immediately took counsel with the renegade about what means we should use to carry off the Moorish lady and bring us all to Christian territory. In the end it was agreed that for the present we should wait for a second message from Zoraida (that was the name of the woman who now wishes to be called Maria), because we saw clearly that she, and no one else, could find a way out of all these difficulties. Once we had decided this, the renegade told us not to worry, that he would either lose his life or restore us to liberty. For four days the baño was crowded with people, so the reed delayed its appearance for four days; but at the end of that time, when the baño was as usual empty, the reed reappeared with a cloth so bulky it promised a happy birth. Reed and cloth came down to me, and I found another paper and a hundred crowns in gold, with no other coin. The renegade was present, and in our cell we gave him the paper to read, which ran as follows:

"I cannot think of a plan, señor, for our going to Spain, nor has Lela Marien shown me one, though I have asked her. All that can be done is for me to give you plenty of gold from this window. Use it to ransom yourself and your friends, and let one of you go to the land of the Christians, buy a vessel there, and come back for the others. He will find me in my father's garden, which is at the Babazon gate near the seashore, where I shall be all this summer with my father and my servants. You can carry me away from there by night without any danger and bring me to the vessel. And remember you are to be my husband, or else I will pray to Marien to punish you. If you cannot trust anyone to go for the vessel, ransom yourself and you go, because I know you will return more surely than any other, since you are a gentleman and a Christian. Try to acquaint yourself with the garden; and when I see you walking out there, I shall know the baño is empty and I will give you plenty of money. Allah protect you, señor."

These were the words and contents of the second paper, and on hearing them each man declared himself willing to be the one ransomed and promised to go and return in scrupulous good faith. I made the same offer too. But the renegade objected to all this, saying he would on no account agree to one being set free before all went together, as experience had taught him how badly those who were set free kept the promises they had made in captivity. Captives of distinction frequently used this trick, he said, paying the ransom of one who was to go to Valencia or Majorca with money to fit out a bark and return for the others who had ransomed him — only never to come back; for recovered liberty, and the dread of losing it again, wipe from the memory every obligation in the world. To prove what he said, he told us briefly what had happened to a certain Christian gentleman almost at that very time — the strangest case that had ever occurred even there, where astonishing and marvellous things happen every moment. In short, he ended by saying that what could and ought to be done was for us to give him the money intended for the ransom of one of us Christians, so that he could buy a vessel in Algiers under the pretext of becoming a merchant trading at Tetuan and along the coast. As master of the vessel it would be easy for him to find some way of getting us all out of the baño and on board, especially if the Moorish lady gave, as she said, enough money to ransom us all — because once free it would be the simplest thing in the world for us to embark even in broad daylight. But the great difficulty was that the Moors do not allow any renegade to buy or own any craft, unless it be a large vessel for raiding expeditions, because they fear that anyone who buys a small vessel, especially a Spaniard, only wants it to escape to Christian territory. He could get around this, however, by arranging with a Tagarin Moor to share with him in buying the vessel and in the profit on the cargo. Under this cover he could become master of the vessel, in which case he considered all the rest as good as done. Now, although my comrades and I thought it would be a better plan to send to Majorca for the vessel, as the Moorish lady suggested, we did not dare oppose him, fearing that if we did not do as he said he would denounce us and put us all in danger of losing our lives, if he revealed our dealings with Zoraida, for whose life we would have all given our own. So we resolved to put ourselves in the hands of God and in the renegade's; and at the same time an answer was sent to Zoraida, telling her we would do everything she advised, since she had given us as good counsel as if Lela Marien had spoken it, and that it depended on her alone whether we deferred the business or carried it out at once. I renewed my promise to be her husband; and so, the next day the baño chanced to be empty, she gave us at different times, by means of the reed and cloth, two thousand gold crowns and a paper saying that the next Juma — that is, Friday — she was going to her father's garden, but that before she went she would give us more money. If it was not enough we were to let her know, and she would give us as much as we asked, because her father had so much he would not miss it, and besides she kept all the keys.

We at once gave the renegade five hundred crowns to buy the vessel, and with eight hundred I ransomed myself, giving the money to a Valencian merchant who happened to be in Algiers at the time. He had me released on his word, pledging that on the arrival of the first ship from Valencia he would pay my ransom; for if he had handed over the money at once it would have made the king suspect that my ransom money had been in Algiers for a long time, and that the merchant had kept it secret for his own gain. In fact my master was so hard to deal with that I dared not on any account pay the money down at once. The Thursday before the Friday on which the fair Zoraida was to go to the garden, she gave us another thousand crowns and warned us of her departure, begging me, if I were ransomed, to find out her father's garden at once and to seek every opportunity of going there to see her. I answered briefly that I would do so, and that she must remember to commend us to Lela Marien with all the prayers the captive woman had taught her. This done, steps were taken to ransom our three comrades, so as to get them out of the baño; for otherwise, seeing me ransomed and themselves not, even though the money was forthcoming, they might make a fuss about it, and the devil might prompt them to do something that would harm Zoraida. Although their station might have been enough to relieve me of this fear, I was unwilling to take any risk in the matter, and so I had them ransomed in the same way I was, handing over all the money to the merchant so that he could give security with safety and confidence — without, however, confiding our arrangement and secret to him, which might have been dangerous.
